findings.paper_title: Appendix. 3a for 2026/27 CAPITAL BUDGET – QUARTER 2 FORECAST OUTTURN
findings.headline: £2.845m of the Ashton Public Realm budget is ringfenced for Ashton Streetscape/Albion Way, with proposals still under discussion with TfGM.
findings.detail: The paper says proposals for the area 'remain under discussion with TfGM given the potential impact on bus journey times.' The next milestone is a workshop with TfGM to identify deliverable options for Albion Way, planned for Sep 26.
findings.matters: Ringfenced capital that has no agreed project yet, pending a transport authority's view, is a timing and deliverability risk that other councils with ringfenced regeneration funds would recognise.

findings.paper_title: Appendix. 3a for 2026/27 CAPITAL BUDGET – QUARTER 2 FORECAST OUTTURN
findings.headline: Stalybridge Civic Hall (Victoria Market Hall) internal works: the final Phase 2 item, replacement of fire doors, is stated as due for completion by end September 2026.
findings.detail: The paper says all other Phase 2 works are complete. It records no actual date for Phase 2 completion, which was planned for Dec 25. The paper does not confirm whether the end-September 2026 date was met.
findings.matters: A procurement delay on the last element of a £1.000m refurbishment shows where a supply chain issue has pushed a completion date back.
findings.figures: £1.000m whole scheme total; £0.266m 2026/27 budget and projected outturn; £0.096m actual to date
findings.quote: the replacement of remaining fire doors which were heavily delayed due to procurement issues.

findings.paper_title: Appendix. 3a for 2026/27 CAPITAL BUDGET – QUARTER 2 FORECAST OUTTURN
findings.headline: Stalybridge Capital Regeneration Projects forecasts £5.257m of 2026/27 spend, while the paper gives the £19.9m grant's delivery date as 31 March 2026.
findings.detail: The scheme has a £6.535m 2026/27 budget with £1.225m actual to date. Stalybridge West enabling works are planned to start on site in Jan 27 and Astley Cheetham completion is planned for Mar 27. The paper does not say whether the 31 March 2026 date has been extended.
findings.matters: A council still spending heavily on a grant with a stated end date that has passed would need to confirm the grant terms with the funder, and peers would want to know the outcome.

findings.headline: LUF funding for Ashton can now be used up to March 2028, with the formal funding profile changed.
findings.detail: The paper records no actual date yet for the Market Square public realm completion, planned for Sep 26, or for Casey's construction completion, planned for Apr 26. It says the majority of the public realm space will be available in Q3 26/27.
findings.matters: An extension of the spend deadline on a £19.870m Levelling Up Fund scheme is a change in the programme's timing risk that other councils with LUF schemes would compare.

findings.paper_title: Appendix. 3a for 2026/27 CAPITAL BUDGET – QUARTER 2 FORECAST OUTTURN
findings.headline: Godley Garden Village: £0.212m slip requested because estimated legal and surveyors' fees have reduced in year.
findings.detail: The paper says the reduction is because not all of the anticipated legal work has been needed. The S106 agreement was signed in March 2026 against a February 2026 plan, and the reserved matters application was submitted in April 2026 as planned.
findings.matters: A £5.808m garden village scheme slipping money because legal work came in lower shows how enabling costs can move before infrastructure starts.
findings.figures: £0.397m 2026/27 budget; £0.185m projected outturn; (£0.212m) variation; £5.808m whole scheme total
findings.quote: Approval to slip £0.212m is requested as the estimated costs to cover legal fees and surveyors fees for Godley Green have reduced in year as it has not been necessary to undertake all of the legal work anticipated.

findings.paper_title: Appendix. 3a for 2026/27 CAPITAL BUDGET – QUARTER 2 FORECAST OUTTURN
findings.headline: Denton Festival Hall: works are not progressing while the future owner and use are unknown, and £2.456m of Denton LUF 2026/27 budget reprofiling is requested.
findings.detail: Watertight works had been due to go to procurement in September 2026. After expressions of interest from parties interested in buying the hall, the Council decided not to progress them. The paper says the circa £2.2m allocated to Festival Hall in 2026-27 is unlikely to be spent this year.
findings.matters: A £16.765m Levelling Up Fund scheme is reprofiling spend because a disposal decision is pending, which affects the timing of cash and any grant conditions.

findings.quote: It is now very unlikely that this will be spent this financial year.

findings.detail: The new approvals table records the switch as a change in funding source, shown as Borrowing (£8.589m). The paper says the move follows Executive Cabinet decisions.

findings.headline: St Annes Denton Primary's £0.392m secure entrance scheme has a grant agreement date ending in October 2026, with an extension request to follow the planning decision.
findings.detail: The scheme is rated RED. Designs are awaiting final sign-off from the planning department, and the Trust has not yet provided a programme of works.
findings.matters: A grant agreement expiring before the scheme has a programme of works means the grant extension becomes a dependency for delivery.

findings.paper_title: Appendix. 3c for 2026/27 CAPITAL BUDGET – QUARTER 2 FORECAST OUTTURN
findings.headline: St Stephen's RC Primary School's specialist resource provision cost rises from a £0.850m allocation to £0.950m.
findings.detail: All tender returns came in above the original allocation. The paper attributes the increase to relocating the modular building after a protected greenspace area was identified. Exec Cabinet approved the extra £0.100m in July 2026, and £0.425m is requested to be reprofiled from 2027/28.
findings.matters: A scheme cost rising by about 12% after tender, with the extra funding approved by Executive Cabinet, is a common pattern in council primary SEND and resource base projects.

findings.paper_title: Appendix. 3c for 2026/27 CAPITAL BUDGET – QUARTER 2 FORECAST OUTTURN
findings.headline: Meadow View Children's Home's works completion moves from February to March 2027, and the DfE has extended grant expenditure into 2026/27.
findings.detail: The contractor reports being about two weeks behind, which moves the completion month from February to March. The children's home opening date is shown as TBC. The project had been paused while the DfE considered the extension request.
findings.matters: A grant-funded children's home slipping by a month, with the grant deadline extended to cover it, shows how external grant deadlines shape capital delivery for councils building in-house care.

findings.headline: Childcare Expansion Grant projects £0.115m against a £0.325m budget, and £0.211m is requested for reprofiling into 2027/28.
findings.detail: One early years scheme has been removed, reducing the allocation to £0.341m, of which £0.293m has been paid. Three further enquiries did not provide the grant information needed for panel approval and are no longer progressing.
findings.matters: Grant funding for childcare places is going unspent when providers do not come forward, which is a recurring risk for councils managing un-ringfenced capital grants.

findings.paper_title: Appendix. 3c for 2026/27 CAPITAL BUDGET – QUARTER 2 FORECAST OUTTURN
findings.headline: Cromwell High School's additional places scheme projects £1.000m against a £0.500m budget, and £0.500m is requested to be slipped into 2026/27 from 2027/28.
findings.detail: The original satellite site was ruled out because the roof would need replacing to meet building regulations, which the paper calls 'extremely costly'. The council relocated a modular building and reconfigured Rayner Stephens rooms instead. findings.headline: Longdendale High School's £0.863m 2026/27 budget projects nil spend, and the full amount is requested for reprofiling into 2027/28.

findings.paper_title: Appendix. 3d for 2026/27 CAPITAL BUDGET – QUARTER 2 FORECAST OUTTURN
findings.headline: The Housing Adaptations case management system is costed at £24,232 plus VAT over 24 months, and its IT governance approval is still to be completed before an October/November 2026 implementation.
findings.detail: The paper says the current digital case files are vulnerable to corruption and take up a lot of storage. It states the cloud system costs £23,682 plus £550 customisation, totalling £24,232 plus VAT, for 1 October 2026 to 30 September 2028. The Digital Board passed the report, but IT Governance did not form part of the decision-making.
findings.matters: A system purchase proceeding ahead of completed IT governance is a control point that finance and audit teams elsewhere would want to see closed.

findings.paper_title: Appendix. 3d for 2026/27 CAPITAL BUDGET – QUARTER 2 FORECAST OUTTURN
findings.headline: The Ask Sara portal is due to end in December 2026, so the council will not implement it and is looking for a replacement.
findings.detail: The paper says the Shaw Trust has provided information that the Ask Sara system will end in December 2026. The portal was intended to direct people with low-level adaptation needs to an online shop. Research into a similar product is ongoing, and the milestone to start it was June 2026.
findings.matters: A planned digital channel for low-level adaptations is being dropped before implementation because the third-party service is closing, which affects the demand-management approach other councils may also be taking.
findings.quote: Information has been provided by the Shaw Trust Ask Sara system will be ending in December 2026, therefore this system will not be implemented.

findings.paper_title: Appendix. 3d for 2026/27 CAPITAL BUDGET – QUARTER 2 FORECAST OUTTURN
findings.headline: The Housing Adaptations Team reports 124 referrals, 213 approvals and 175 completions for April to September 2026, and says demand continues to exceed its capacity.
findings.detail: The paper says the number of cases awaiting allocation is rising steadily. It lists 266 Minor Works requests and 234 Minor Works completions for the same period. It also describes a new database, a fast-track process for bathroom adaptations, and proposed new posts and regraded roles to add capacity.

findings.paper_title: Appendix. 4 for 2026/27 REVENUE BUDGET – MONTH 6 FORECAST OUTTURN
findings.headline: Interest receivable is forecast at £0.782m against a £4.442m budget, an adverse variance of £3.660m, which the council attributes to lower average cash balances.

findings.paper_title: Appendix. 4 for 2026/27 REVENUE BUDGET – MONTH 6 FORECAST OUTTURN

findings.matters: The adverse receivable shortfall is larger than the favourable payable saving, so the net position is adverse, and this pattern is relevant to any council relying on investment income.

findings.quote: Overall, the net interest position is forecast to be £4.201m payable against a net budget of £2.176m payable, representing an adverse variance of £2.025m.

findings.headline: Capital expenditure forecast for 2026/27 is £79.413m, against £61.856m in the Treasury Management Strategy.

findings.paper_title: Appendix. 4 for 2026/27 REVENUE BUDGET – MONTH 6 FORECAST OUTTURN
findings.headline: Council says early repayment of some PWLB loans, which are in or close to a discount position, is not necessarily cost-effective.
findings.detail: Gilt yields have risen since early 2022, so some PWLB loans are in or close to a discount position if repaid early. The council says repaid loans would potentially need replacing at higher rates, so restructuring is not necessarily cost-effective. Any restructuring would be supported by Arlingclose.
findings.matters: Lenders and finance officers would see that a discount on early repayment does not automatically make restructuring worthwhile when replacement funding costs more.

findings.quote: However, as the repaid loans would potentially need to be replaced by new loans at higher interest rates, this isn't necessarily a cost-effective option for the Council.

findings.paper_title: Appendix. 4 for 2026/27 REVENUE BUDGET – MONTH 6 FORECAST OUTTURN
findings.headline: Short-term borrowing from other local authorities cost 3.8% to 5.5% over the quarter, above Bank Rate of 3.75%, and costs rose throughout the period.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the high short-term rates to many authorities relying more on the short-term market to avoid expensive long-term rates. It also cites low cash levels and the non-receipt of SEND grants as likely contributors to high borrowing demand.
findings.matters: Rising short-term costs affect the cost of funding a council's liquidity gap, and the same market pressure applies to peers relying on short-term loans.
findings.figures: 3.8% to 5.5% short-term cost; Bank Rate 3.75%; short-term borrowing £15.000m at 30 September 2026 (£5.000m at 30 June 2026); weighted average return 4.27%.
findings.quote: The cost of short-term borrowing from other local authorities has been above Bank Rate during the period at 3.8% to 5.5% and costs have risen throughout the period.

findings.paper_title: Appendix. 4 for 2026/27 REVENUE BUDGET – MONTH 6 FORECAST OUTTURN
findings.headline: The £10m Dexia LOBO was replaced with a £10m two-month loan from Greater Manchester Combined Authority, after the council consulted Arlingclose.
findings.detail: The council took a short-term loan from another local authority on the advice of Arlingclose. findings.matters: The replacement was short-term rather than long-term PWLB funding, so the council's refinancing exposure moved to the short-term market.

findings.quote: This was done in the form of a £10m 2 month loan from Greater Manchester Combined Authority.

findings.detail: Audits of Preparation for Adulthood, EHCPs, and Be Well all received Limited Assurance ratings, meaning the systems of governance, risk management and control require improvement to effectively manage risks. These audits collectively identified 21 agreed actions (7, 3, and 11 respectively), with 9 Priority 1 actions requiring immediate attention.
findings.matters: Multiple Limited Assurance opinions in high-risk council services (children's services and wellbeing) indicate internal controls are not operating effectively to manage significant risks; this concerns both finance directors assessing management capability and lenders evaluating whether the council can reliably manage public resources.
findings.figures: 3 Limited Assurance reports issued; Preparation for Adulthood 7 actions (3 Priority 1); EHCPs 3 actions (2 Priority 1); Be Well 11 actions (4 Priority 1)

findings.headline: MTFP forecast shows budget gap growing from £6.964m in 2027/28 to £53.862m by 2030/31
findings.detail: The Medium Term Financial Plan projects cumulative budget gaps of £6.964m in 2027/28, £15.907m in 2028/29, £37.686m in 2029/30, and £53.862m by 2030/31. findings.matters: The rapid growth of budget gaps indicates structural financial problems requiring substantial service changes or revenue growth, not one-off savings or temporary measures.

findings.headline: Council implemented Budget Recovery Plan to reduce £15m overspend by 31 March 2027
findings.detail: Tameside has activated enhanced financial controls and recovery measures effective immediately, including corporate expenditure controls, recruitment and workforce controls, accelerated savings delivery, and income maximisation initiatives. The target is to reduce the forecast overspend of £15.054m to zero by 31 March 2027.

findings.paper_title: Budget Update - Scrutiny Coordination & Strategic Improvement Scrutiny Panel - 210926
findings.headline: 2026/27 savings delivery off-track: 84.7% forecast achievement; 72.7% of target rated at-risk
findings.detail: Of £19.129m in approved savings for 2026/27, only £16.210m is forecast to be achieved (84.7%). £13.9m of the required savings (72.7%) is rated amber (at risk), £2.919m (15.3%) is rated red (not on track), and only £0.748m (3.9%) has been achieved to date.

findings.headline: Council Tax collection from Council Tax Support recipients fell to 76.69% in 2025/2026 from 81.22% in 2022/2023, 19 percentage points below 95.6% national average

findings.paper_title: Appendix. 1 for Council Tax Support Scheme 2027-2028
findings.headline: Annual cost of Council Tax Support scheme rising from £15.9m in 2024/25 to £19.2m estimated in 2026/27, a 20.8% increase outpacing recipient growth
findings.detail: The scheme cost £15.9m in 2024/25, rising to £17.4m in 2025/26 (a £1.5m increase in one year) and estimated at £19.2m for 2026/27 (a further £1.8m increase). findings.paper_title: ITEM 6 - Treasury Management Outturn Report
findings.headline: Tameside holds a large £37.4m exposure to Manchester Airport Group via a shareholder loan with accumulated deferred interest.
findings.detail: The council has lent £29.632m as a shareholder loan to Manchester Airport Group, with a further £8.954m of deferred and accrued interest from COVID-related deferrals, totalling £37.440m outstanding. While this generated £4.735m in distributions during 2025/26, it represents a large concentrated exposure to a single entity in a historically volatile sector.
findings.matters: A concentrated exposure to a single economically-sensitive entity and sector represents material risk to council finances, particularly if airport operations or dividend capacity deteriorate.
findings.figures: £29.632m principal shareholder loan; £8.954m deferred/accrued interest; £37.440m total outstanding; £4.735m distributions received in 2025/26
findings.quote: Tameside Council lent £29.632m to Manchester Airport Group. Due to COVID, interest payments were deferred, but recommenced in March 2023. As at 31 March 2026, deferred and accrued interest equated to £8.954m.

findings.paper_title: ITEM 6 - Treasury Management Outturn Report
findings.headline: The council continues to hold £30m of LOBO loans carrying semi-annual call options, creating ongoing refinancing risk.
findings.detail: Beyond the Dexia loan already called, Tameside holds a further £30m of LOBO loans with call options exercisable twice yearly. The probability of lenders exercising these options increases as interest rates remain elevated. This creates a stream of potential refinancing decisions and cost exposures across 2026/27 and beyond.
findings.matters: Embedded call risk creates multiple refinancing decision points and exposes the council to potential cost escalations if rates do not fall as forecast.
findings.figures: £30m LOBO loans with semi-annual call options; weighted average return 4.42%; weighted average maturity 30.4 years
findings.quote: At 31 March 2026, the Council continued to hold £30m of LOBO loans where the lender has the option to propose an increase in the interest rate at set dates, following which the Council has the option to either accept the new rate and terms or to repay the loan.

findings.paper_title: ITEM 6 - Treasury Management Outturn Report
findings.headline: Interest income fell 19% short of budget at £0.886m, driven by falling rates and declining cash balances.
findings.detail: The council earned £3.789m in investment interest against a budget of £4.675m. This shortfall was caused by both lower interest rates throughout the year and the deliberate use of cash balances to fund capital rather than invest. This represents a revenue pressure on the council's budget.
findings.matters: Interest income shortfalls indicate revenue exposure to external economic factors and reduce resources available for service delivery or debt repayment.
findings.figures: Interest earned £3.789m; budgeted £4.675m; variance of £0.886m (19% underspend)
findings.quote: Interest income of £3.789m was earned against a budget of £4.675m, an unfavourable variance of £0.886m. Falling cash balances through the year and interest rate reductions were significant drivers of interest income being lower than forecasted.

findings.paper_title: ITEM 6 - Treasury Management Outturn Report
findings.headline: Investment reserves have fallen by 64% as the council used cash balances to fund capital expenditure and defer borrowing.
findings.detail: The council's investment balance fell from £62.640m to £22.030m, a reduction of £40.610m. While this reflects a deliberate strategy to avoid borrowing during a period of elevated interest rates, it materially reduces the council's financial cushion and flexibility for future needs or unexpected demands.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the council's remaining liquidity and financial flexibility to handle future capital needs or service shocks.
findings.figures: Investment balance fell from £62.640m to £22.030m (reduction of £40.610m, or 64%)
findings.quote: Investment balances decreased by £40.610m during the year, reflecting the deferral of borrowing decisions and the use of existing cash balances, capital receipts, reserves and grants to fund capital expenditure.

findings.paper_title: ITEM 6 - Treasury Management Outturn Report
findings.headline: A £5m LOBO loan from Dexia has been called and requires immediate refinancing as interest rates increased.
findings.detail: On 16 June 2026, Dexia exercised its option to increase the rate on a £5m LOBO loan. The Section 151 Officer has elected to prepay the principal in full and consider refinancing options. This is the start of potential refinancing activity across the council's broader £30m LOBO portfolio, which carries semi-annual call options.
findings.matters: Refinancing needs represent active debt management challenges and potential cost escalation at a time when interest rates remain uncertain.
findings.figures: £5m Dexia LOBO called; £30m LOBO loans remaining with semi-annual call options
findings.quote: Dexia, lender of a £5m LOBO loan with an option date of 16 June 2026, has exercised the option to increase the rate on the loan and the Section 151 Officer has elected to prepay the principal in full and consider refinancing options.

findings.detail: The council identifies that increasing market pressures and significant forthcoming contract renewals have exposed weaknesses in commissioning and contract management. The paper commits to strengthening the contract management framework, improving commercial capability, and ensuring consistent oversight of strategic suppliers to secure value for money and manage risk.

findings.detail: The paper identifies that capital programme delivery continues to be affected by multiple issues: slippage, cost escalation, and dependency on external funding. The council acknowledges a need to strengthen programme management, improve forecasting accuracy, and enhance governance oversight to ensure timely and effective delivery.
findings.matters: Capital programme slippage and cost escalation affect financial planning, the council's ability to deliver service improvements, and forecasting accuracy for medium-term financial planning
findings.figures: Capital programme affected by slippage, cost escalation, external funding dependency
findings.quote: The delivery of the capital programme continues to be affected by slippage, cost escalation and dependency on external funding. This creates risks to both financial planning and service delivery outcomes.

findings.detail: The council identifies that pressures within Adults and Children's Services, combined with slippage in the capital programme, create a specific risk to in-year budget control. findings.quote: Pressures within Adults and Children's Services, alongside slippage in the capital programme, present a risk to in-year budget control.

findings.headline: Material DSG high-needs deficit represents a longer-term financial sustainability risk
findings.detail: The council explicitly identifies that the Dedicated Schools Grant high-needs deficit has reached a material level. This risk increased following the cessation of the statutory override, which previously allowed councils to avoid accounting for DSG deficits. The paper commits to developing and implementing a DSG deficit recovery strategy but flags this as a critical medium-term financial issue requiring enhanced oversight.
findings.matters: A growing DSG deficit that cannot be offset by statutory override is a structural financial risk to the council and affects medium-term financial sustainability

findings.paper_title: Appendix 11 - Treasury Management Strategy
findings.headline: Revenue budget overspends are eroding cash reserves alongside lower investment income
findings.detail: The council's treasury investment balance has fallen significantly from prior years, with average investments of £62.5m in 2025/26 to end-December 2025. The council explicitly notes that revenue budget overspends are contributing to these lower cash balances, indicating current operational pressures.
findings.matters: Ongoing budget overspends indicate operational challenges and reduce the council's financial flexibility and reserves available to manage future risks or changes
findings.figures: Average treasury investments £62.5m (lower than 2024/25); range £36.9m-£86.7m in 2025/26
findings.quote: The impact of revenue budget overspends may also contribute to lower cash balances.

findings.headline: Capital expenditure forecast to fall 99% from £61.856m in 2026/27 to £0.4m in 2027/28
findings.detail: The treasury strategy states capital expenditure will increase and require unwinding of internal borrowing. findings.quote: The Council's internal borrowing position may need to be unwound over the forecast period as capital expenditure increases, which will require new loans to be taken.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 11 - Treasury Management Strategy

The council will then need to either accept higher rates or repay the loans using internal resources.

findings.paper_title: Budget Report 2026-27
findings.headline: Council requires relentless execution focus on transformation and full budget rebuild in 2027/28 to have any chance of closing future budget gaps
findings.detail: The Section 151 Officer's statement emphasises the council 'must ensure a relentless focus on delivery of its budgeted proposals and the full budget rebuild for 2027/28, to have any chance of closing the gap in future years.' This language indicates material execution risk and acknowledges that closure of future years' gaps is not assured.
findings.matters: Indicates significant dependency on successful transformation programme execution over the next 12 months. Slippage in transformation or failure to rebuild budget assumptions from 2027/28 will result in further deterioration.

findings.paper_title: Budget Report 2026-27
findings.headline: 88% of council tax base in bands A–C limits revenue-raising capacity from tax increases
findings.detail: Tameside has an unusually low-banded property portfolio with 88% of its council tax base in bands A–C. This structural limitation means each percentage increase in council tax yields less revenue than it would for councils with higher-value properties.
findings.matters: Limits financial flexibility to address future budget gaps through local revenue raising. Reduces options to manage structural deficit in years beyond 2026/27.
findings.figures: 88% of tax base in bands A–C; Council Tax 42% of total resources in 2026/27; Band D equivalent tax base 65,683.2 properties
findings.quote: Tameside has 88% of its Council Tax base in Bands A – C. This impacts on the Council's ability to raise funds from this source.

findings.paper_title: Budget Report 2026-27
findings.headline: Council services experiencing unprecedented levels of demand and complexity in core areas including Adults, Children's, temporary accommodation and SEN transport
findings.detail: The report attributes to 'the cost-of-living crisis and current economic climate' ongoing 'unprecedented levels of demand and complexity of need at the front door' in key service areas. The council has invested £23.103m to address these pressures.
findings.matters: Indicates structural, ongoing cost drivers in high-volume service areas that cannot be easily dismissed as temporary. Investment alone may not resolve underlying demand.
findings.figures: £23.103m investment to address demand and complexity growth; £8.230m demographic investment in 2026/27
findings.quote: Due to the impact of the cost-of-living crisis and current economic climate, Council services are still seeing unprecedented levels of demand and complexity of need at the front door.

findings.paper_title: Budget Report 2026-27
findings.headline: 2026/27 budget assumes unproven demand management will offset £8.230m demographic and complexity investment in Adults, Children's, temp accommodation and SEN
findings.detail: The budget includes £8.230m demographic investment in high-cost, volatile service areas (Adults, Children's Services, temporary accommodation, SEN transport) but assumes demand management and cost avoidance measures within directorates will offset this investment. The report explicitly states this will be 'closely monitored during 2026/27 to ensure that these budgets are manageable and deliverable', signalling uncertainty.
findings.matters: These are high-need, volatile services with documented unprecedented demand levels. If demand management does not deliver as assumed, there will be in-year pressure in the largest budget areas.
findings.figures: £8.230m demographic investment 2026/27; £23.103m total investment in services experiencing significant growth in pressures
findings.quote: As such demand management and cost avoidance measures are assumed within the relevant department budgets to offset the total investment required. This will be closely monitored during 2026/27 to ensure that these budgets are manageable and deliverable in 2026/27 and beyond.

findings.paper_title: Budget Report 2026-27
findings.headline: Section 151 Officer warns reserve draw-down over recent years 'is not sustainable in the long run'
findings.detail: The Section 151 Officer's statement acknowledges reserves have been used to 'provide services with the time to improve, but this is not sustainable in the long run.' This indicates services given time to stabilize through reserve use have not achieved financial balance.
findings.matters: Reserves are a finite, one-off resource. Continued reliance indicates unresolved structural budget problems in service areas and reduced cushion against future shocks.
findings.figures: Proposed minimum general fund balance £15.707m (5% of budget); proposal to transfer £5.008m to reserves in 2026/27
findings.quote: The Council has made use of reserves over the last few years, to provide services with the time to improve, but this is not sustainable in the long run and the Council needs to ensure robust and transparent transformation of services, and reduction of demand, to ensure the delivery of the improvement plans in place.

findings.paper_title: Budget Report 2026-27
findings.headline: 2026/27 balance depends entirely on delivery of £8.973m savings with no contingency buffer
findings.detail: The report explicitly states 'all budget reductions proposed must be delivered in full in-year' to balance the budget. The opening budget imbalance was £8.973m, exactly matched by identified savings. There is no contingency for partial delivery or implementation delay.
findings.matters: Any shortfall in savings delivery will immediately create an in-year budget crisis. The council has no flexibility to absorb delivery risks.
findings.figures: £8.973m savings required; £314.133m balanced budget requires 100% delivery
findings.quote: To deliver this balanced net budget, all budget reductions proposed must be delivered in full in-year and Council approves a maximum increase in Council Tax.

findings.paper_title: Budget Report 2026-27
findings.headline: 2025/26 currently tracking £9.2m overspend despite £6m contingency allocated for inflation pressures that have not materialised
findings.detail: Latest month 9 monitoring shows £9.2m overspend. The council had allocated £6m contingency for inflation impacts that have not occurred, yet remains significantly over budget. This suggests underlying demand or complexity pressures in service areas rather than temporary cost spikes.
findings.matters: Current financial year shows inability to control expenditure within approved budget even in a favorable inflation environment, raising concerns about service cost discipline.
findings.figures: £9.2m month 9 overspend in 2025/26; £6m contingency already used
findings.quote: The latest 2025/26 monitoring position is forecasting a £9.2m overspend against budget at month 9. This is after utilisation of £6m of contingency funds pre-dominantly allocated to support potential in year inflationary increases across Council services which will no longer materialise in the current financial year.

findings.paper_title: Budget Report 2026-27
findings.headline: Significant budget gap emerging in 2027/28 and beyond that will worsen if savings do not deliver
findings.detail: The Section 151 Officer's formal statement warns of a significant budget gap beyond 2026/27 and notes the gap will 'only increase if planned savings, transformations and efficiencies are not delivered.' The council's stated focus is 'short-term balance in 2026/27' with 'a full budget rebuild for 2027/28 and beyond', indicating the current-year balance is tactical rather than structural.
findings.matters: The budget appears balanced only through one-year measures and does not represent a sustainable underlying position. Future years show increasing imbalance that requires unspecified additional savings.
findings.figures: £314.133m balanced budget 2026/27; budget gap from 2027/28 unquantified; full rebuild needed 2027/28 onwards
findings.quote: However, the Council faces a significant budget gap beyond 2026/27, and this budget gap will only increase if planned savings, transformations and efficiencies are not delivered.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 7 - Reserves Strategy
findings.headline: The council expects reserves will be needed to cover future budget gaps if savings targets are not achieved
findings.detail: The reserves strategy identifies future budget gaps as a specific reason reserves may be drawn down, explicitly conditioning this on an absence of additional savings or funding sources.
findings.matters: Relying on reserves to bridge structural deficits is unsustainable; it signals the baseline budget is under pressure
findings.figures: None specified in document
findings.quote: Future budget gaps may require reserves in the absence of additional savings or funding.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 7 - Reserves Strategy
findings.headline: Children's Social Care has historically driven significant reserve drawdowns
findings.detail: The council explicitly identifies that significant reserve funding has already been consumed in prior years due to unexpected costs and demand pressures in Children's Social Care, indicating an ongoing structural pressure in this major spending area.
findings.matters: A recurring service pressure that depletes reserves signals that budget assumptions for this service are not holding
findings.figures: None specified in document
findings.quote: Significant reserve funding has been used in prior years for unexpected cost and demand pressure in Children's Social Care.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 7 - Reserves Strategy
findings.headline: Most of Tameside's £136.5m in earmarked reserves are already committed to other purposes
findings.detail: While the council holds substantial total reserves (£136.457m as of 1 April 2025), most are committed to existing purposes and a review is planned for 2026/27. This significantly limits the council's financial flexibility for unexpected events or service pressures.
findings.matters: A lender must understand what 'free' reserve capacity actually exists, not just headline totals, to assess the council's ability to absorb shocks
findings.figures: Total Earmarked Funds at 1st April 2025 £136.457m
findings.quote: Whilst the overall level of reserves held by the Council remains strong, most of these reserves are committed and a review will be undertaken during 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 10 - Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Major capital commitments with costs marked TBC: Mayoral Development Corporation and Town Centre Redevelopment lack finalised budgets
findings.detail: Two of the largest proposed investment areas—the Mayoral Development Corporation and Town Centre Redevelopment—have estimated costs marked 'TBC' across all five years of the plan. The Town Centre programme includes £5m annually for strategic property acquisitions but the return or end-state is undefined. These sit alongside the Ashton Town Hall commitment and related regeneration initiatives.
findings.matters: Unfunded or open-ended capital commitments, particularly for acquisition of land or buildings, represent unquantified cash exposure and potential financial risk if market conditions deteriorate or acquisitions do not meet expected returns.
findings.figures: Town Centre Redevelopment: TBC annually; Mayoral Development Corporation: TBC annually; Strategic Acquisitions: £5m annually over 5 years (£25m total)
findings.quote: Mayoral Development Corporation TBC TBC TBC TBC TBC; Town Centre Redevelopment TBC TBC TBC TBC TBC

findings.paper_title: Appendix 10 - Capital Strategy
findings.headline: CCTV infrastructure significantly past operational life, with 40 cameras aged 16+ years when maximum recommended age is 5 years
findings.detail: Of 138 public-realm cameras, 56 are within spec (2–5 years old), but 39 are 6–9 years old and 40 are 16+ years old; additionally, 3 camera locations are inoperable. The council proposes £2m investment in 2026/27 to replace aging cameras and migrate to dark-fibre technology.
findings.matters: Infrastructure aging and service degradation indicate accumulated maintenance arrears; the cost-of-replacement profile signals near-term cash outflows for essential public safety infrastructure.
findings.figures: 40 cameras aged 16+ years (vs. 5-year maximum); 3 inoperable locations; £2m proposed for replacement
findings.quote: Of the 138 public realm cameras mentioned above, 56 are between 2-5 years old, with the maximum recommended age being 5 years old. 39 are between 6-9 years old, the remaining 40 cameras are 16 years old or more, as well as 3 additional locations where the cameras are inoperable.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 10 - Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Ashton Town Hall heritage asset: £22.5m investment committed but council acknowledges significant challenges in securing viable long-term use
findings.detail: The council is investing £22.5m to refurbish the Grade II listed Town Hall (£2.5m in 2026/27, £10m each in 2027/28 and 2028/29), yet explicitly notes significant challenges in finding a sustainable use for the building interior. The building was closed in 2015 and has been vacant for over a decade.
findings.matters: A major capital commitment exists for an asset where the council has not yet identified a viable end-use or revenue model; this represents potential value loss or future write-downs if the investment does not generate anticipated returns.
findings.figures: £22.5m capital investment over three years; building closed since 2015
findings.quote: It is noted that there are significant challenges associated with securing a long term sustainable use for the building interior.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 10 - Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Significant new borrowing planned with revenue cost implications built into MTFS
findings.detail: The strategy explicitly states the council will undertake prudential borrowing to fund capital investment, with borrowing costs factored into the Medium-Term Financial Strategy. The council is proposing £156m of new capital investment over five years (Table 3), against a current programme of £101.5m, substantially increasing debt servicing obligations.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand increased leverage and the revenue budget pressure from higher debt servicing costs, particularly given existing financial constraints mentioned in the MTFS.
findings.figures: Proposed capital investment £156m over 2026/27–2030/31; current programme £101.504m (2025/26–2027/28)
findings.quote: it will be necessary for the Council to undertake borrowing in some cases. The associated costs of borrowing have been factored into the Medium Term Financial Strategy on the basis of current costs estimates for the required levels of investment.

findings.paper_title: 2024-25 Audit Completion Report - Tameside MBC - 250226
findings.headline: Information Commissioner's Office audit found limited assurance with 33 urgent, 49 high, 20 medium and 4 low priority recommendations; Council suffered data breach in December 2025.
findings.detail: Following a consensual ICO audit beginning July 2024, the September 2024 report covered governance and accountability, the Data Protection Officer role, personal data breach management, access requests, and freedom of information. Limited assurance was provided with 106+ recommendations across these five areas. In December 2025, the Council identified that its Waste Offences Register had been inadvertently accessible to the public via the website, resulting in potential exposure of personal data. Immediate action was taken to remove the data and secure affected web pages.
findings.matters: An ICO consensual audit resulting in limited assurance and 33 urgent recommendations, combined with an actual data breach self-identified in December 2025, indicates systemic data governance and compliance weaknesses creating legal and reputational risk.
findings.figures: ICO recommendations: 33 urgent, 49 high, 20 medium, 4 low priority; data breach self-identified December 2025
findings.quote: In summary, across all of these areas a limited assurance rating was provided and identified considerable scope for improvement in existing arrangements.

findings.paper_title: 2024-25 Audit Completion Report - Tameside MBC - 250226
findings.headline: Cash position deteriorated from £102.1m to £17.7m (83% reduction); Council took new short-term loan while increasing investments to £46m.
findings.detail: Cash and cash equivalents decreased from £102.1m in 2023/24 to £17.7m in 2024/25. This was partially offset by an increase in short-term investments from nil to £46m and was driven by capital scheme spending. Short-term borrowings increased from prior year due to a new short-term loan taken out in 2024/25. The sharp decline in actual cash, despite the shift to investments, indicates tighter liquidity conditions.
findings.matters: The Council has drawn down cash reserves by 83% while taking on new short-term borrowing, signalling stressed liquidity and increased reliance on financial markets for short-term funding.
findings.figures: Cash and cash equivalents £17.7m (down from £102.1m); short-term investments £46m (up from nil); short-term borrowings increased due to new short-term loan
findings.quote: The significant decrease in cash and cash equivalents (£17.7m in 2024/25; £102.1m in 2023/24) is partially offset by the significant increase in the short-term investments position (£46 m in 2024/25; nil in 2023/24) and decrease in cash due to spend of capital schemes in 2024/25. The short-term borrowings have increased from prior year due to short-term loan taken out in the year.

findings.paper_title: 2024-25 Audit Completion Report - Tameside MBC - 250226
findings.headline: Asset valuation misstatements of £4.53m (Property/Plant/Equipment) and £1.37m (Investment Properties) identified; PPE audit work remains incomplete.
findings.detail: Through reconciliation between the Council's asset schedules and external valuation reports from Sanderson Weatherall Ltd, the auditor identified that valuations had not been appropriately reflected in the asset register. For Land and Buildings and Surplus assets, a discrepancy of £4.53m was identified and adjusted. For investment properties, a discrepancy of £1.37m was adjusted. Additionally, the auditor had not received all responses from valuers and the Council on valuation queries as of the report date, and therefore could not complete audit work on Property, Plant and Equipment valuation.
findings.matters: £5.9m in identified valuation misstatements plus incomplete audit procedures on a major asset category (£496.2m of PPE) suggests control weaknesses in asset accounting and heightens concerns given the broader unresolved audit issues.
findings.figures: PPE valuation misstatement £4.53m; Investment Properties valuation misstatement £1.37m; PPE book value £496.246m at 31 March 2025 (down from £542.443m, includes £86m derecognition from academisation)
findings.quote: Through this work, we identified that the valuations from the external valuer had not been appropriately reflected the asset register, resulting in a discrepancy of £4.53 million.

findings.paper_title: 2024-25 Audit Completion Report - Tameside MBC - 250226
findings.headline: IFRS 16 PFI transition error required £28.7m material adjustment for incorrect inflation estimates in unitary charge calculations.
findings.detail: During review of the Council's transition of PFI contracts to IFRS 16, the auditor identified that the Council had incorrectly included an estimate for inflation within future Unitary Charge payments. The interpretation of CIPFA Code requires the PFI liability adjustment to exclude any inflation estimates in future years' Unitary Charge payments. The Council developed a revised model, which resulted in a material adjustment of £28.7m to correct the IFRS 16 remeasurements. The Council is currently updating the financial statements to address this matter.
findings.matters: A £28.7m adjustment — material to the accounts — due to misinterpretation of CIPFA Code on a significant accounting change indicates control weaknesses in complex accounting interpretations and the impact of delayed audit procedures on financial statement accuracy.
findings.figures: £28.7m material adjustment required; £34.278m total impact of IFRS 16 in draft statements (£33.076m PFI, £1.202m other PPE)
findings.quote: We raised this issue with the Council, who subsequently developed a revised model. This resulted in a material adjustment of £28.7 million to correctly reflect the IFRS 16 remeasurements.

findings.paper_title: 2024-25 Audit Completion Report - Tameside MBC - 250226
findings.headline: Usable reserves fell £18.2m; General Fund balance dropped £14.6m; Dedicated Schools Grant deficit will reach cumulative £44.5m by March 2026.
findings.detail: Total usable reserves decreased by £18.2m from £154.7m to £136.5m. General Fund balance dropped £14.6m from £125.5m to £110.8m. Earmarked Reserves decreased £14.1m to £74.3m. The DSG deficit increased £14.1m to cumulative £22m at 31 March 2025, driven by growth in demand for Education, Health and Care Plans. The Council forecasts a DSG deficit of £22.4m in 2025/26, increasing the cumulative deficit to £44.5m by 31 March 2026. While the General Fund is maintained at the £27.5m minimum target, the trajectory of reserve depletion is concerning.
findings.matters: Rapid reserve depletion across all categories, particularly a 16% decline in earmarked reserves in one year, combined with a DSG deficit doubling to £44.5m, indicates the Council is consuming financial buffers to fund services and cannot sustain current spending patterns.
findings.figures: Usable reserves £136.5m (down £18.2m year-on-year); General Fund balance £110.8m (down £14.6m); Earmarked Reserves £74.3m (down £14.1m); DSG cumulative £22m at 31 March 2025, forecast cumulative £44.5m at 31 March 2026
findings.quote: In total the usable reserves decreased by £18.2m, from £ 154.7m as at 31 March 2024 to £136.5m as at 31 March 2025.

findings.paper_title: 2024-25 Audit Completion Report - Tameside MBC - 250226
findings.headline: Head of Assurance issued limited assurance opinion on governance for second consecutive year; internal audit team turned over entirely by November 2025
findings.detail: The 2024/25 Internal Audit Annual Report contains a limited assurance opinion from the Head of Assurance — the second consecutive year. This reflects capacity issues in the internal audit team, the July 2024 ICO limited assurance rating, limited assurance on risk management, the external audit disclaimer of opinion, and scope limitations. The internal audit function has suffered critical turnover: the former Head of Assurance left shortly after drafting the report, an interim Head was appointed May 2025, the Senior Auditor left, and the remaining auditor departed November 2025. From 1 April 2026, internal audit will be outsourced to Southwest Audit Partnership.
findings.matters: A limited assurance opinion on internal controls and governance, repeated year-on-year and accompanied by near-total turnover of the audit team, indicates serious weaknesses in the Council's ability to assure its own financial and operational controls.
findings.figures: Limited assurance opinion both 2023/24 and 2024/25; ICO audit: 33 urgent, 49 high, 20 medium, 4 low priority recommendations
findings.quote: In our view, these circumstances provide clear evidence of a significant weakness in the Council's governance arrangements, based on the Head of Assurance's limited assurance opinion on the overall adequacy of the Council's framework of governance, risk management, and internal control for the 2024/25 period.

findings.paper_title: 2024-25 Audit Completion Report - Tameside MBC - 250226
findings.headline: OFSTED rated Children's Services 'inadequate'; February 2025 monitoring visit found improvements had not been made; Department for Education issued improvement notice in March 2025.
findings.detail: OFSTED inspection in February 2024 concluded overall effectiveness is inadequate. A monitoring visit on 13–14 February 2025 found required improvements had not been made. A joint OFSTED and CQC SEND inspection found services have not improved fast enough. The Department for Education issued an improvement notice in March 2025 for poor progress against the SEND Written Statement of Action. The auditor identified a continuing significant weakness in the Council's arrangements for governance and improving economy, efficiency and effectiveness in respect of Children's Services.
findings.matters: Children's Services failure is driving the largest budget overspend (£16.4m in 2024/25, £7.175m forecast 2025/26) and formal regulatory intervention by DfE indicates sustained service delivery failure with no clear recovery trajectory.
findings.figures: Children's Social Care £16.4m overspend 2024/25; £7.175m forecast overspend 2025/26; inadequate OFSTED rating February 2024; DfE improvement notice March 2025
findings.quote: A monitoring visit to Tameside's Children's Services was made on 13 and 14 February and found the improvements needed had not been made since the last inspection.

findings.paper_title: 2024-25 Audit Completion Report - Tameside MBC - 250226
findings.headline: Revenue budget overran by £16.9m in 2024/25, funded from reserves, with £9.2m forecast overspend in 2025/26 despite £19.7m savings targets.
findings.detail: The Council overspent its 2024/25 budget by £16.9m, primarily driven by Children's Social Care (£16.4m overspend: £10.6m external placements, £6.7m staffing). For 2025/26, the budget requires £19.7m savings plus £3.2m unachieved from prior years, but only £3.564m achieved by period 9. A forecast overspend of £9.201m is predicted after recovery plans, with £11.341m of savings rated red (high delivery risk). The Council acknowledges that using reserves to fund overspends is not sustainable.
findings.matters: Two consecutive years of large budget overruns funded from reserves, combined with failed savings delivery (only 18% achieved), indicates structural spending problems that reserves cannot sustain indefinitely.
findings.figures: 2024/25 overspend £16.9m; 2025/26 forecast overspend £9.201m; Children's Social Care 2024/25 overspend £16.4m; 2025/26 savings £19.7m required plus £3.2m brought forward, only £3.564m achieved, £11.341m rated red
findings.quote: The council recognises the use of reserves to fund overspends is not sustainable and council needs to ensure that savings are implemented in full or permanent reductions in expenditure are identified without delay.

findings.paper_title: 2024-25 Audit Completion Report - Tameside MBC - 250226
findings.headline: Auditor has issued a disclaimer of opinion on the 2024/25 financial statements, following a disclaimer in 2023/24, due to inability to rebuild sufficient audit evidence on opening balances.
findings.detail: This is the second consecutive year the auditor cannot express an opinion on the Council's financial statements. The auditor could not obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence relating to opening balances of assets, liabilities and reserves. Although most planned audit work was completed, time constraints to meet the statutory backstop deadline of 27 February 2026 prevented completion of procedures needed to rebuild assurance on opening balances carried forward from the prior-year disclaimed statements. The auditor judges the impact to be both material and pervasive.
findings.matters: Unaudited accounts for two consecutive years represent a material governance failure and create fundamental uncertainty about the Council's true financial position — a critical issue for lenders making credit decisions.
findings.figures: £14.1m materiality threshold; statutory backstop deadline 27 February 2026
findings.quote: In our judgement, the impact of the unresolved matters is both material and pervasive, and as such a disclaimer of opinion is required.

news_drafts.headline: Tameside forecasts £70.863m schools grant deficit at March 2027, from £43.873m a year earlier
news_drafts.lead:
Tameside Council forecasts that its dedicated schools grant (DSG), the government grant that funds schools, will carry a cumulative deficit of £70.863m at March 2027, up from £43.873m at 31 March 2026. The figures are in the month 6 budget monitoring, the in-year check of spending against budget, for the Executive Cabinet. The 2025/26 in-year deficit was £21.783m, which the paper attributes to overspends in high needs, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND), from growth in Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCPs).

The in-year high needs deficit for 2026/27 is forecast at £27.630m, against £29.772m in the original budget and £27.927m forecast in June. Government proposes to fund 90% of deficits accrued to 31 March 2026, subject to Department for Education approval of Tameside's SEND reform plan, submitted in summer 2026. The council expects to hear in early autumn. The council must provide the remaining 10%, plus an estimated 10% of the 2026/27 and 2027/28 deficits, whose proportions are not yet confirmed. It estimates a call on reserves, money set aside, of around £11m.

The statutory override, a temporary government rule that lets councils keep a schools-funding deficit off their main balance sheet, is set to expire after 2027/28. The five-year forecast has in-year high needs deficits rising to £51.853m by 2030/31 without significant reforms to funding and net reductions in EHCP numbers. The council expects significant SEND deficit funding in the third quarter of 2026/27, which it says "should support deferral of external borrowing". It has deferred a long-term refinancing decision, taking new loans to repay old ones, on expectations of rates falling. Short-term borrowing stood at £15m at 30 September 2026.

news_drafts.headline: Tameside repaid £5m Dexia LOBO loan at par after lender proposed 6.68% rate, up from 4.5%
news_drafts.lead:
Tameside Council has repaid a £5m bank loan early rather than accept a higher interest rate, its Audit Committee was told on 22 September. The loan was a LOBO (a bank loan where, on set dates, the lender may propose a higher interest rate and the council may then repay the loan in full instead of accepting it). The lender, Dexia, exercised its option and proposed raising the rate from 4.5% to 6.68% from 16 June 2026. The council repaid the principal at par, meaning in full with no extra charge.

The loan had an option date every six months and would have run to 2054. The council's quarterly treasury management report (treasury management is how a council borrows, invests its spare cash and manages the risks of both) says replacement loans of the same length were available from the PWLB (Public Works Loan Board, the government's lending arm for councils) at 6.28%, lower than the rate Dexia proposed.

The council did not take a long-term loan. It paid Dexia with £5m of short-term borrowing from other local authorities at 4.3%, which the paper describes as deferring a commitment to long-term rates. The repayment leaves £25m of LOBO loans, all of which still carry call options every six months.
